content: General anaesthesia is typically associated with a state of unconsciousness. However, awareness refers to instances where patients have postoperative recall of events or experiences that occurred during surgery. In contrast, wakefulness describes situations where patients regain consciousness during surgery but do not have any postoperative recollection of this period of consciousness. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of two types of anaesthetic interventions in reducing clinically significant awareness during surgery. These interventions included: (1) specific anaesthetic drug regimens and (2) the use of intraoperative anaesthetic depth monitors. To gather relevant data, the researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase, covering studies published up to April 2016. They also contacted experts to identify additional studies and manually reviewed citations. However, trial registries were not searched. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated either anaesthetic drug regimens or anaesthetic depth monitors. Studies involving volunteers, patients prior to skin incision, intensive care unit settings, or those focused solely on memory tests without anaesthetic interventions were excluded. Anaesthetic drug regimens included studies on both induction and maintenance of anaesthesia. Anaesthetic depth monitors evaluated in the study included devices such as the Bispectral Index (BIS) monitor, M-Entropy, Narcotrend monitor, cerebral function monitor, cerebral state monitor, patient state index, and lower oesophageal contractility monitor. These monitors are used to titrate anaesthetic drugs to maintain unconsciousness during surgery. Data collection and analysis involved at least two authors independently reviewing abstracts, extracting data, and assessing the risk of bias in the included studies. The authors also contacted study investigators for clarification when needed. Meta-analyses were performed using statistical packages in the R programming language. The review included 160 studies with a total of 54,109 participants. Of these, 53,713 participants began the studies, and 50,034 completed them or were included in data analysis. However, 115 RCTs could not be used in meta-analyses because they reported zero awareness events. Additionally, 27 studies were excluded from pooling due to significant clinical and methodological heterogeneity. Ultimately, 18 RCTs with 36,034 participants were included in the meta-analyses. In the analysis comparing anaesthetic depth monitoring (using either the Bispectral Index or M-Entropy) to standard clinical and electronic monitoring, nine trials with 34,744 participants were included. The overall event rate of awareness was 0.5%. The results showed no significant difference between anaesthetic depth monitoring and standard monitoring in reducing awareness, with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.98 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 1.62), indicating low precision in the estimate. A subset analysis of five studies focused on Bispectral Index monitoring versus standard monitoring, involving 34,181 participants. In this subset, 503 participants reported awareness events, which were adjudicated by a blinded expert panel. The panel categorized the reports as no awareness (351 cases), possible awareness (87 cases), or definite awareness (65 cases). The effect size did not favor either Bispectral Index monitoring or standard monitoring for the combined outcome of definite and possible awareness (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.65). For definite awareness alone, the effect size slightly favored Bispectral Index monitoring, but the precision was low (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.13 to 2.75). Three smaller meta-analyses focused on anaesthetic drug regimens, including nine studies with 1,290 participants. The findings indicated that ketamine and etomidate reduced the incidence of wakefulness compared to thiopental. Wakefulness was observed to occur more frequently than awareness. Benzodiazepines were found to reduce the risk of awareness compared to thiopental, ketamine, and placebo. Additionally, higher doses of inhaled anaesthetics were associated with a lower risk of awareness compared to lower doses. The quality of evidence for the five comparisons was graded as low or very low in the Summary of Findings tables. Most secondary outcomes were not reported in the included RCTs. In conclusion, anaesthetic depth monitors may have effects similar to standard clinical and electronic monitoring in reducing the risk of awareness during surgery. In older studies involving a smaller subset of patients, wakefulness was more common than awareness. The use of etomidate and ketamine was associated with a lower risk of wakefulness compared to thiopental. Benzodiazepines, as well as higher doses of inhaled anaesthetics, were found to reduce the risk of awareness.
